definition: Lacking the drive, skill, or sense of duty needed to get things done.
example: His feckless cousin borrowed money to start a bakery and spent it all on concert tickets.
nuance: Feckless faults a lack of purpose or competence, while the look-alike reckless faults dangerous, careless boldness.
prompt: A team leader keeps missing deadlines on a group project for science class.
options: The feckless leader promised a schedule every week but never wrote one down.
The feckless leader sped through the parking lot at twice the posted limit.
The feckless leader finished every task early and organized the rest of the team.
The feckless leader did everything right but lost the files when a storm cut the power.
reasons: Making empty promises and never following through shows weak, aimless leadership.
Dangerous daring is recklessness, a look-alike word, not a failure to get things done.
Early, well-organized work is the opposite of ineffectual behavior.
Bad luck despite real effort is hapless; this word blames a person's character.

practice.prompt: A town committee is responsible for repairing a broken footbridge over a creek.
options: The feckless committee repaired the bridge within a week and came in under budget.
The feckless committee sent workers onto the bridge during a flood without safety lines.
Residents thanked the feckless committee for its firm, dependable leadership on the project.
After months of meetings, the feckless committee had still not hired a single carpenter.
reasons: Fast, thrifty results show competence, which reverses the meaning.
Taking careless risks is recklessness; the word describes doing too little, not acting rashly.
The word is always a criticism, so it cannot describe leadership worth praising.
Endless talk without action is exactly the ineffectiveness the word criticizes.
